title: Post-restore validation harness and TF snippets for private deployments
content:
Purpose:
This working draft describes a lightweight, repeatable post-restore validation harness and supporting Terraform notes for Private deployments (VPC/on-prem). Goal is to provide a checklist + small test harness that can be re-run after any backup restore (partial, full, or cluster-level) to assert that the deployment is functional and safe to bring back into production.

Scope:
- Applies to on-prem and VPC private deployments managed by our Terraform modules and the private control plane.
- Focused on: data-plane restore (datastore, object store snapshots), stateful service metadata (KV caches, feature flags), and basic API surface health.
- Not covering full chaos testing or application-level correctness tests (those live in solutions-eng test suites), but includes pointers for where to call those.

Assumptions and prerequisites:
- Restore has completed: block level snapshots restored or object snapshots available and mounted.
- Terraform has been applied to provision infra where required (EBS/LVM volumes, mounts, network interfaces). We assume the restore step used the existing TF modules but may have temporarily overridden some inputs.
- Access: operator has kube/ssh access to nodes and access to the private control plane.
- RPO/RTO targets: RPO <= 1h for hosted critical tables; RTO target for full cluster restore = 4 hours (target in contract). Adjust expectations per customer.

High-level validation phases (fast path):
1) Sanity checks (5-15m): credentials, mounts, process health.
2) Data integrity checks (15-45m): checksums, row counts, keyspace reconciliation.
3) Service-level smoke tests (15-60m): API endpoints, readiness probes, simple inference queries, and KV cache warming.
4) Observability and telemetry validation (10-30m): logs, traces, and metrics ingestion to ensure alerts are meaningful.

Phases details and commands (examples):
- Sanity checks:
  - Confirm restored volumes are attached and mount points exist: mount | grep /var/lib/redwood-data; df -h.
  - Verify owner/perm bits for data dirs: ls -al /var/lib/redwood-data; chown as required.
  - Process checks: systemctl status redwood-api || docker ps | grep redwood || kubectl get pods -n redwood.
  - Credential and secrets presence: kubectl -n redwood get secret redwood-kms --output=jsonpath='{.data.kmsKey}' || check KMS access in cloud VPN.

- Data integrity checks (examples):
  - Database row counts: psql -h <db> -c "select count(1) from requests where created_at > now() - interval '30 days';"
  - Spot-check primary keys / keyspace: run small script that randomly samples 100 keys and validates they exist in index and object store. We store a manifest file during backup: /backups/manifest-<timestamp>.json. Use that for comparisons.
  - Checksum verification for object store snapshots: sha256sum -c /backups/objects-<ts>.sha256 (or provided tool).
  - Kafka / Redis AOF validation: redis-check-aof /var/lib/redis/appendonly.aof; kafka log directory offsets vs manifest.

- Service-level smoke tests:
  - Health endpoints: curl -sSf https://internal-api.redwood.local/health || fail. Check components: store, kv, runtime.
  - Inference smoke: run a lightweight model call with small input and validate shape and tokens returned. Use a replay dataset in tests/replay/smoke.json.
  - Admin checks: ensure routing rules / config loaded: kubectl -n redwood get cm routing-config -o yaml and scan for expected model ids.
  - KV cache warming: execute a set of pre-saved prompts to populate cache and validate cache hit metrics increment (see metrics below).

- Observability validation:
  - Confirm metrics pipeline: curl prometheus:9090/api/v1/query?query=up and validate redwood_job metrics present.
  - Logs: ensure fluentd/rsyslog forwarding is up and logs for recent restarts include no data-migration failures.
  - Traces: sample a request and check tracer shows end-to-end span.

Acceptance criteria (minimum):
- All critical services report healthy (health endpoint shows ok)
- Datastore row counts within +/- 1% of backup manifest or reconciliation script passes tolerance thresholds.
- Object store checksums OK or documented exceptions (e.g., missing ephemeral indices)
- Smoke inference returns valid shaped output for 5/5 attempts within latency budget (for smoke)
- Metrics and logs are being scraped/forwarded and a subset of alerts fire in a known-good state (no new unresolved critical alerts)

Validation harness design notes (lightweight executable):
- Small Python CLI (validate_restore.py) that runs phases and aggregates a JSON result. Should be idempotent and safe to run on restored instances.
- CLI outputs: {status: PASS|WARN|FAIL, checks: [ {name, state, message} ], artifacts: [paths-or-urls] }
  - We will keep a copy of the last 7 run artifacts in /var/backups/restore-validation/ for on-prem.
- Exit codes: 0 = PASS, 2 = WARN (can be triaged), 3 = FAIL (blocker).

Terraform module notes and snippets:
- Goal: make restore-time changes minimal and preferably handled by targeted runbooks rather than wholesale TF changes. Where TF changes are needed, prefer small, reversible modules.

- Common patterns we use in PRs:
  - data "external" "snapshot_manifest" { program = ["/usr/local/bin/parse-manifest", var.snapshot_path] }
  - module "restore_volume" { source = "git::ssh://git.internal.redwood/infra-mods.git//modules/restore-volume?ref=stable" customer = var.customer_id snapshot = var.snapshot_id }

- Notes on Terraform state and idempotency:
  - When restoring block devices into an existing TF-managed machine, avoid re-creating resources. Use terraform import for volumes if the restore preserved resource ids. Document process: terraform import module.restore_volume.aws_ebs_volume.volume vol-xxxxx.
  - For air-gapped on-prem, we prefer using a temporary vars file (restore.tfvars) and a local state file during the restore to avoid stomping production remote state. Example workflow: terraform init; terraform apply -var-file=restore.tfvars -state=restore-<ts>.tfstate; after verification migrate changes to the main state with terraform state rm/add as needed.

- Example TF snippet for a safe LVM attach wrapper (pseudo):
  - resource "null_resource" "attach_lvm" { provisioner "local-exec" { command = "/usr/local/bin/attach-lvm.sh ${var.volume_device} ${var.mount_point}" } }

Upgrade plan considerations and restore compatibility:
- Upgrades that change on-disk formats must include migration and rollback scripts. During restore we must detect version mismatch between restored filesystem/schema and code being started.
- Policy: always bring up the previous running release if the restore contains older-format data. Only perform in-place data migrations after a successful validation on the previous release.
- Backward-compatibility checklist for upgrade-with-restore:
  - Are DB schema migrations reversible? (yes/no + link to migration PR)
  - Are model shard formats stable across releases?
  - Is there a preflight tool to detect incompatible object manifests?

Drill plan and cadence:
- Quarterly full-restore DR drill for Dedicated customers (simulate region failure): recovery team executes full restore to an isolated VPC; run validation harness; produce post-mortem within 48h.
- Monthly partial drills (single service or snapshot) for internal readiness.

Post-restore runbook checklist (operational):
- Step 0: Tag the restore: create ticket with snapshot id, operator, start time.
- Step 1: Mount and permissions check.
- Step 2: Run validate_restore.py --phase=sanity, capture logs to ticket.
- Step 3: Run data integrity checks: run manifest comparator.
- Step 4: Start core services in maintenance mode, run smoke tests.
- Step 5: If PASS -> remove maintenance mode, monitor 2x normal alert sensitivity for 2 hours.
- Step 6: If WARN -> escalate to on-call SRE and eng-resilience owner.
- Step 7: If FAIL -> rollback to snapshot and re-evaluate restore path; if impossible, escalate to incident lead.

Metrics to collect during validation:
- restore.duration.seconds (per phase)
- validation.check.*.latency and success_rate
- disk.read_errors, disk.write_errors during initial workload
- model.inference.smoke.latency

Open questions / TODOs:
- Determine standard manifest format and where to persist manifests for on-prem (S3 equivalent on customer side).
- Add replay dataset for each customer to the backup policy (privacy review required).
- Hook validate_restore.py to the Console to surface results in the restore job UI (backend API design needed).

References and links:
- Internal PR for restore-volume module: https://git.internal.redwood/infrastructure/pull/1234
- DR runbook index: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/ENG/Private+Deployments+DR+Index
- Related Jira: JIRA-OPS-987

Quick edit log:
- 2025-11-12 A. Patel initial draft
- 2026-01-07 R. Menon added TF import notes and idempotency guidance
- 2026-02-25 E. Garcia added acceptance criteria and metrics

Notes to self:
- When we stabilize the manifest format, add a small Go utility to do fast manifest diffs (avoid Python for large 100k-object manifests).
- Consider a ‘dry-run-restore’ mode that mounts snapshots readonly and runs validation without touching production state.
